volumes.title: Wagons on the Lowlands Road
volumes.text:
Wren Hallow saw them first, because the bakery on Cross Street has the highest attic window in Emberwick and she had been watching from it since Tuesday. On Thursday, a little after four, the Lowlands road grew a smudge of smoke. Under the smoke came a traction engine painted plum and gold, and behind the engine seven wagons, nose to tail like ducklings.

She was down three flights and into the shop before the flour settled. Marrable’s are coming, she said. Her father went on shaping loaves. They came every year in the last week of September, he said, and every year she announced it as if it were news.

It was news. Wren stood on the step with flour to her elbows and counted them in over the Ember bridge. Seven wagons. On the last, under a tarpaulin, something stuck out that looked very like a wooden hoof.

volumes.title: The Green by Lamplight
volumes.text:
Marrable’s Travelling Fair takes one night to build, and most of Emberwick has never seen it done, being asleep. Wren Hallow, eleven, the baker’s daughter, saw it because bakers rise at three. She carried the first tray of rolls across to Goose Green in the dark and stopped dead at the gate.

The Green was full of lanterns and quiet grumbling. Men walked about with striped poles on their shoulders. A woman in a leather apron, who turned out to be Bess Marrable, stood on the engine and directed everything with a spanner. In the middle, the roundabout was going up like a great umbrella opening, rib by rib.

Bess bought all the rolls. Then she looked at Wren, who had not moved, and handed her a mallet. The pegs for the hoopla stall wanted knocking in, she said, and they would not knock themselves.

volumes.title: Opened by the Mayor
volumes.text:
The Goose Fair at Emberwick cannot begin until the Mayor has declared it open, a rule the Mayor is fond of. So at noon on Friday the whole of Marrable’s Travelling Fair stood ready and silent on Goose Green, the roundabout still, the coconuts waiting on their cups, while Mayor Tibbet read a speech.

It covered the charter of the fair, the price of geese, and the new drain in Mill Lane. Wren Hallow, at the front with her father’s tray of buns, watched a showman fall asleep standing up. Then came the ribbon, and it was found that nobody on the Committee had brought scissors. There was a conference. Wren held up the bakery bread knife.

The Mayor sawed through the ribbon in eleven strokes. Bess Marrable pulled a lever, the engine whistled, and every stall on the Green shouted at once.

volumes.title: Eleven Horses and a Pole
volumes.text:
The roundabout at Marrable’s Fair is called the Gallopers, and it is the reason most of Emberwick comes to Goose Green in fair week. Wren Hallow, the baker’s daughter, rode it on the Friday evening with the first of her four saved pennies. Her horse was dapple grey with a scarlet saddle, and on a scroll along its neck was painted a name: Candlewade.

They all had names. Thrushby, Oddmoor, Saltgrave, Kettlebridge. Old Jem Marrable, who took the pennies, told her each horse was carved in a town on the fair’s road and called after it, one a year when he was young and slower since. Wren counted as they went round. Eleven horses. And one brass pole, twisted like barley sugar, going up and down with nothing on it.

She asked whose that was. Jem said it was nobody’s yet, and let her go round again.

volumes.title: Three Balls a Penny
volumes.text:
On the Saturday of fair week, Wren Hallow, the baker’s daughter, spent two of her three remaining pennies at the coconut shy, and has regretted one of them ever since.

The shy at Marrable’s Fair is kept by a mournful man named Mr Dabb, who calls out three balls a penny as though announcing bad weather. Wren’s first three balls struck the canvas, the grass, and Mr Dabb’s bucket. Her second three were worse. One coconut rocked, considered the matter, and stayed. Mr Dabb said she had a baker’s arm, good for kneading, and offered no further comment.

She walked home by the edge of Goose Green. The great limb the lime tree dropped in the March gale still lay there, since the Parish Committee had met six times about it without deciding anything. Old Jem Marrable stood beside it in the dusk, running his thumb along the grain.

volumes.title: Sixpence and a Ride
volumes.text:
Marrable’s Fair does not open on a Sunday. Goose Green was quiet, the stalls shuttered, the eleven horses of the roundabout hanging still under their canvas. So the whole Parish Committee had leisure to gather round a fallen lime limb and be asked a question by an old showman.

Jem Marrable wanted to buy it. Lime, he said, was the best carving wood there was, and this piece had a horse in it. The Committee conferred. Mr Pim had always favoured a bench. Mrs Garland favoured firewood for the almshouse. The Mayor favoured a further meeting. Wren Hallow, delivering Sunday rolls from the bakery, heard them settle at last on sixpence and one free ride apiece.

Jem paid on the spot. By the time the Committee had finished shaking hands with one another, he had fetched an adze and taken off the first long curl of bark.

volumes.title: Rain on the Canvas
volumes.text:
It rained all Monday. Marrable’s Fair sat on Goose Green under dripping awnings, the straw trodden to porridge, the coconut man playing patience on an upturned bucket. Wren Hallow had one penny left and nowhere dry to stand, so she ducked into the smallest tent, which had a painted sign: Madame Zephyrine Sees All.

Madame Zephyrine was Mrs Marrable in a shawl with coins on it. She was turning the heel of a sock. She said fortunes were a penny, but she would not take a last one, and that she could tell it was a last one by the way it was being held.

So they drank tea instead, and listened. Behind the tent, under a tarpaulin stretched from the roundabout, came a steady knock and pause, knock and pause. That was Jem, Mrs Marrable said, finding out where the horse’s head was.

volumes.title: A Horse in the Wood
volumes.text:
By Tuesday of fair week the fallen lime limb from Goose Green had a neck. Old Jem Marrable, who carves the horses for his own roundabout, worked at it behind the Gallopers with a mallet and three gouges, and Wren Hallow came after the morning bake to sweep up for him.

She learned a good deal by sweeping. The horse would be a jumper, legs tucked, ears laid back as if it heard the organ. The head was made separately and pegged on. The shavings smelled of honey and were to go to the bakery for kindling, which Jem called a fair trade for rolls.

At noon the Parish Committee arrived to inspect their limb. Mr Pim thought the nose long. Mrs Garland wondered if it might smile. Jem thanked them, went on cutting, and changed nothing at all, and they left well pleased with their contribution.

volumes.title: The Colour of a Crust
volumes.text:
A roundabout horse is only timber until it is painted, and on the Wednesday of fair week the question of what colour to paint the new one nearly divided Emberwick. It had been carved on Goose Green by old Jem Marrable from the town’s own lime tree. The town felt entitled to a view.

The Mayor proposed civic blue. The fishermen up from the Grey Coast said grey, like weather. Somebody’s aunt held out for piebald. Bess Marrable, who mixes the fair’s paint in jam jars, listened with a brush behind her ear and then asked Wren Hallow, who had swept up every shaving and said nothing.

Wren thought. Brown, she said. The brown of a loaf when it is just right, with a mane the colour of the inside. Bess looked at the horse, then at the bakery chimney across the Green, and reached for the burnt umber.

volumes.title: The White of the Eye
volumes.text:
On Thursday evening the twelfth horse of Marrable’s roundabout stood on two trestles behind the fair, loaf-brown, with a cream mane and a saddle of green and gold. Wren Hallow, the baker’s daughter, had come every day to watch it made. It had everything now but a name and a look in its eye.

Bess Marrable lettered the name on the neck scroll, freehand, in gold with a red shadow: Emberwick. Then old Jem did a thing Wren did not expect. He loaded the smallest brush with white, put it in her hand, and pointed. One dot, he said, high in the dark of the eye. Not the middle. That was the difference between a horse and a hat stand.

Her hand shook. She breathed out, as she did before slashing a loaf, and touched the brush down once. The horse looked at her.

volumes.title: First Ride
volumes.text:
The last night of the Goose Fair is always the best, and this one had a new horse in it. At dusk on Friday four showmen carried the loaf-brown jumper round to the Gallopers and hung it on the brass pole that had gone up and down empty all week. Twelve horses at last, on a roundabout built for twelve.

Then came the matter of who should ride it first. The Mayor felt the office spoke for itself. The Parish Committee produced their free tickets and a point of order. The custom of the fair, said old Jem Marrable, was that a new horse is first ridden by whoever swept up after it.

Wren Hallow paid her last penny anyway, on principle. The organ struck up, the lamps blurred into one gold ring, and the horse called Emberwick carried her round above the hats of the whole town.

volumes.title: The Ring on the Grass
volumes.text:
A fair goes faster than it comes. By ten on Saturday morning Marrable’s had folded itself back into seven wagons, and Wren Hallow stood at the gate of Goose Green with a parcel of rolls for the road, which Bess Marrable was for once not allowed to pay for.

The engine whistled. The wagons swung out over the Ember bridge towards the Lowlands, nose to tail. On the last one, under the tarpaulin, a brown hoof stuck out. Old Jem lifted his hat from the tailboard and called that she should look for them in the last week of September, and bring her sweeping arm.

Then the road was empty. On the Green there was a wide pale ring where the roundabout had stood, and a clean scar on the lime tree where the limb had been. Wren walked once round the ring, slowly, and went home to the ovens.

volumes.title: The Sixty-First Fire
volumes.text:
Annals of the Emberwick Bonfire Society, kept by Ambrose Tuck, Recorder, newly elected, there being no other candidate.

For those who come after: on the last night of October the Society lights a fire on Beacon Head. It does so in memory of the Long Fog, when the herring fleet was fogbound off the Grey Coast and the town burned its own chairs and tables on the headland to bring the boats home. Each household still gives one piece of old furniture to the stack. That is the whole of the custom, and the Committee has forty-one rules concerning it.

Sixty-first fire. Weather clear, wind light, westerly. Stack fourteen feet, measured by the Treasurer with a marked pole. Lit at seven. A fire was also observed across the bay on the Nab, where the village of Skerrin keeps the same night. It appeared to us somewhat smaller.

volumes.title: Mrs Pargeter's Sideboard
volumes.text:
Annals of the Emberwick Bonfire Society. Sixty-second fire on Beacon Head, last night of October. Ambrose Tuck, Recorder. Weather cold and still. Stack fifteen feet.

The Society must record an incident. By custom each household gives one piece of worn-out furniture to the fire. Mr Pargeter of Tanner’s Row gave a sideboard. It emerged at twenty minutes to seven, by way of Mrs Pargeter arriving on the headland at some speed, that the sideboard was neither worn out nor his to give, being her mother’s, and having her best tablecloths still in the left-hand drawer.

Six members took the stack down to the fourth layer and got it out. The fire was lit forty minutes late. The Committee has since passed Rule Forty-Two: no gift accepted unless countersigned by every adult of the household. Mr Pargeter gave a footstool instead, and was not thanked.

volumes.title: The Wet Year
volumes.text:
Annals of the Emberwick Bonfire Society, which each last night of October burns old furniture on Beacon Head in memory of the Long Fog. Sixty-third fire. Ambrose Tuck, Recorder.

It rained for nine days beforehand and through the evening itself. The stack, thirteen feet and sodden, was offered a light at seven. It declined. It declined again at half past, and at eight, by which hour Skerrin’s fire across the bay was burning clearly on the Nab, and their chapel bell was heard ringing, we thought unnecessarily.

At ten past nine the Treasurer went down to the Society’s cupboard and returned with eleven years of his own accounts, which he said nobody had ever asked to see. They were dry. The fire caught at nine-forty and burned till two. The Recorder notes that these annals were not offered, and will in future be kept in a different cupboard.

volumes.title: A Question of Feet
volumes.text:
Annals of the Emberwick Bonfire Society. Sixty-fourth fire, Beacon Head, last night of October. Recorder, Ambrose Tuck. Fine and frosty. Stack sixteen feet, our tallest in living memory.

Word then came by the carrier that Skerrin, whose fire stands on the Nab across the bay, was claiming eighteen. The Committee does not concern itself with rivalry. It did, however, send the Treasurer and his marked pole round by the coast road the next morning, purely in the interests of accuracy.

His report is entered in full. The Skerrin stack had stood on a natural hummock of some four feet, which their Committee had counted in. Their own Treasurer, met on the spot, replied that Beacon Head is ninety feet above the sea and nobody had ever asked us to subtract it. The two gentlemen measured each other’s poles, found a difference of one inch, and parted without settling whose.

volumes.title: Three Hundred Potatoes
volumes.text:
Annals of the Emberwick Bonfire Society, concerning the sixty-fifth fire lit on Beacon Head on the last night of October. Kept by Ambrose Tuck, Recorder. Weather mild. Stack fifteen feet.

This year a Refreshments Sub-Committee was formed, consisting of Miss Dunnock and whoever stood nearest. Three hundred potatoes were pushed into the edge of the embers at eight o’clock with a rake. At nine it was found that nobody had marked where. A general search by lantern recovered forty-four, of which the Committee ate eleven in the course of confirming they were done.

The remainder were discovered at first light by the children of the town, who needed no sub-committee and found every one, cold, black, and by their account perfect. Parkin was also served. Rule Forty-Three now requires that potatoes be counted in and counted out. Skerrin, we hear, had sausages.

volumes.title: The Hedgehog Inspection
volumes.text:
Annals of the Emberwick Bonfire Society. Sixty-sixth fire. Ambrose Tuck, Recorder. Dry, with a sharp east wind. Stack fifteen feet and, in the Recorder’s view, the best built yet.

A stack of old furniture standing three weeks on Beacon Head is, to a hedgehog, a furnished house. Miss Dunnock therefore proposed that the whole be searched before lighting, and conducted the search herself on the last afternoon of October with a lantern, a long spoon and a lined basket. The Society records her findings: three hedgehogs, asleep in a chest of drawers; one tabby cat, not asleep, and of the opinion that it lived there; and Mr Pim of this Committee, also asleep, who had sat down in a donated armchair at noon to guard the stack.

All were removed to safety. The Hedgehog Inspection is now Rule Forty-Four. The fire was lit at seven and burned cleanly.

volumes.title: The Old Question
volumes.text:
Annals of the Emberwick Bonfire Society, sixty-seventh fire. Ambrose Tuck, Recorder. Weather fair. Stack fifteen feet.

Both this town and the village of Skerrin across the bay light a fire each last night of October, we on Beacon Head and they on the Nab, and each has always held that it was their fire that brought the herring boats home in the Long Fog. This year the Skerrin schoolmaster printed a pamphlet saying so. The Recorder accordingly spent three evenings in Emberwick Library with the harbour book of that year.

The entry is short. It gives the date, the fog, the number of boats, and then, in the harbourmaster’s hand: all came in on the fires. The Recorder notes the word fires. He takes it for a slip of the pen, the man having been up all night, and has written to the schoolmaster to say the matter is closed.

volumes.title: Mr Flint's Fountain
volumes.text:
Annals of the Emberwick Bonfire Society. Sixty-eighth fire on Beacon Head, last night of October. Kept by Ambrose Tuck, Recorder. Clear, no wind. Stack fourteen feet.

It was put to the Committee that a plain fire was old-fashioned, and that Mr Flint the chemist could provide a firework. The vote was five to four. Mr Flint arrived with a single item the size of a tea caddy, named by him the Emberwick Fountain, and asked everyone to stand a long way back, which they did.

The Fountain gave a cough, a quantity of pink smoke, and one green star, which rose about a yard, considered Beacon Head, and went out. There was polite applause. Mr Flint bowed. The fire was then lit in the ordinary manner and was greatly admired, and the Committee has resolved by nine votes to none that the Society’s business is bonfires.

volumes.title: The Lean Year
volumes.text:
Annals of the Emberwick Bonfire Society, which burns old furniture on Beacon Head each last night of October. Sixty-ninth fire. Ambrose Tuck, Recorder.

After sixty-eight fires the town has run short of furniture it can spare. This year’s gifts came to a hat stand, two stools and a clothes horse. The Committee looked at them for some time. The Recorder then gave his late aunt’s whatnot, the Treasurer a desk, and Miss Dunnock a chair she said had never liked her. The stack reached nine feet.

Two days before the night, a wagon came round the coast road from Skerrin, loaded with driftwood, and a card: with the compliments of the Nab. The Committee debated for an hour whether this was kindness or comment. It was accepted by one vote. The Recorder must state that it burned blue and green at the edges, and was the handsomest fire in years.

volumes.title: Applewood for the Nab
volumes.text:
Annals of the Emberwick Bonfire Society. Seventieth fire on Beacon Head. Ambrose Tuck, Recorder. Still and starry. Stack fourteen feet, the town having turned out its attics for the anniversary.

Mindful of the driftwood sent us last year by the village of Skerrin, whose own fire burns on the Nab across the bay, the Committee voted to return the courtesy. A cart of applewood from the Lowlands orchards went round by the coast road, with a card. The wording of the card took two meetings. It reads: from Beacon Head.

A joint supper of the two societies was proposed, and debated warmly as to which side of the bay should have it. It was held on neither. But at eight o’clock the wind brought the smell of apple smoke across the water from the Nab, and the Recorder observed several members of this Committee standing quite still, facing it.

volumes.title: A Hand with the Book
volumes.text:
Annals of the Emberwick Bonfire Society, seventy-first fire, Beacon Head, last night of October. Weather kind. The Recorder, Ambrose Tuck, did not measure the stack this year and finds he does not mind.

He has kept this book eleven years, and the path up the headland has grown steeper in that time, though the Committee assures him it has not. He therefore asked for an assistant. Miss Nell Pargeter of Tanner’s Row was appointed, being the only applicant and the best. She carried the book and the lantern up, and he carried himself.

For her use he sets down what he knows. Build it loose in the middle. Chairs burn better than tables. Light it on the windward side and then leave it alone. The rest is in the rules, of which there are now forty-six, and she need not learn them all at once.

volumes.title: Both Fires
volumes.text:
Annals of the Emberwick Bonfire Society. Seventy-second fire. Fog came in off the Grey Coast at dusk, the thickest in memory, and the herring boat Second Thoughts was still out.

We lit at seven on Beacon Head. Skerrin lit on the Nab. Theirs was a soft orange blur across the bay, and ours, they tell us, the same. At nine the boat came in between them, slow and quite safe, late for nothing but supper. Her skipper, Dan Corrie, was puzzled to be asked how. One fire on each shoulder, he said, and you are in the channel. With one alone you go round the bay till morning. His grandfather had it from his.

So it took both, and always did. The harbour book said fires. The Recorder, Ambrose Tuck, was wrong for five years and is glad of it. This is his last entry. Nell Pargeter has the book.

volumes.title: Last in Line
volumes.text:
My name is Odo Fenn. I am a tinsmith, and on the longest night of the year I am the Tail-Lamp of the Emberwick Lantern Parade, which means I walk last. Somebody must. A parade without a back end goes on losing children until morning.

It is a quarter to five and dark at Fell Gate, at the top of the town. They are gathering. Turnip lanterns, paper stars on sticks, a tin moon I made for the schoolmistress. I have forty candle ends in my left pocket and a tinderbox in my right, and my own lamp, which is plain, with a horn window and a good hood.

Twenty years I have done this. We go down through the town to the Ember bridge, every lantern lit, and I count them out at the top and in at the bottom. Tonight I make it two hundred and six.

volumes.title: One Flame from the Forge
volumes.text:
Every lantern in the Emberwick parade is lit from one flame. That is the rule, and I, Odo Fenn, who walk at the back as Tail-Lamp, am the one who enforces it, mostly by frowning.

The flame comes from the forge at Fell Gate. The smith brings out a single taper, shielding it with a hand like a shovel, and lights the lantern nearest the door. That one lights two more. Those light four. I stand on the horse trough and watch it spread down the lane, yellow dot by yellow dot, until the dark at the top of the town has gone soft and gold and smells of hot turnip.

It takes eleven minutes. A boy from Chandler’s Yard tries to use his own match, and I see him, and he knows I see him. He blows it out and queues. The last lantern lit is mine.

volumes.title: The Owl and the Pike
volumes.text:
There are two great lanterns in the Emberwick parade, and they do not get on. I am Odo Fenn, the Tail-Lamp, last in the line, and from the back I have the best view of the quarrel.

Fell Gate builds the Owl. She is willow and paper, nine feet tall, with six carriers inside and eyes that glow amber. The Quay builds the Pike, fourteen feet of green tissue on hoops, carried on poles by eight fishermen so that it swims. Each has led the parade. Each holds that it ought to lead it every year. Nobody has written down whose turn it is, on purpose.

Tonight they settle it as usual, by standing side by side in the mouth of Stair Lane, which is wide enough for one. The Committee is sent for. I sit down on the horse trough with my lamp between my boots, and wait.

volumes.title: Order of March
volumes.text:
The Lantern Parade Committee meets once a year, in the street, in the dark, on the longest night, to decide who goes first. I have watched it for twenty years from the back, where I walk as Tail-Lamp, and it has never taken less than a quarter of an hour.

The Owl of Fell Gate and the Pike of the Quay stand jammed shoulder to fin at the top of Stair Lane. Mrs Garland, presiding, proposes alphabetical order. The Quay asks whether that is O for Owl or F for Fell Gate. Mr Pim consults last year’s minutes by the light of a turnip and finds they say only: resolved, after discussion.

Two hundred lanterns are burning down. In the end a boy of six with a jam jar on a string is asked to choose. He points at the Pike, because it is green. We move off.

volumes.title: Under the Baker's Sign
volumes.text:
We are a third of the way down. I am Odo Fenn, tinsmith, walking last in the Emberwick Lantern Parade with my lamp and my pocket of candle ends, and ahead of me the whole line has stopped again.

It is the Owl. Fell Gate has built her nine feet tall this year, and the bakery sign on Cross Street hangs at eight and a half. She is wedged under it by the ears. The six carriers inside cannot see out and are being given advice by forty people at once. Mr Hallow the baker leans from his upstairs window in his nightcap and offers to butter her.

In the end the carriers kneel, all six together, and the Owl bows low to the bakery and shuffles under. One ear is bent. From the Pike’s crew, waiting below, comes a cheer that is not entirely kind.

volumes.title: The Corner by the Library
volumes.text:
The wind lives at the corner by Emberwick Library. Every year it waits there for the Lantern Parade, and every year I, Odo Fenn, who walk last as the Tail-Lamp, come round that corner to find a third of the lanterns out and the children holding them up to me like empty cups.

This is the work. I kneel with my back to the gust, open the horn window of my lamp, and light them one from another: a paper star, two turnips, a fish on a stick. Eleven candle ends go from my pocket. Somebody inside the library has set a lamp in the long window, and it is a help to see by.

The last is a jam jar on a string, belonging to a boy of six named Pip Garland. His wick is drowned in wax. I pick it clear with a pin, and it takes.

volumes.title: Soup in the Square
volumes.text:
Halfway down the town the Lantern Parade halts in Market Square for soup. I am the Tail-Lamp, Odo Fenn, and I arrive last, as I am meant to, when the best of the dumplings have gone.

The square is a bowl of light. Two hundred lanterns are propped on the steps of the cross, hung from the pump, held between knees. The town band plays something slow, with the cornet a little ahead of the rest. The Owl of Fell Gate and the Pike of the Quay have been stood at opposite ends, like relations at a wedding, and each crew is explaining to its neighbours how the other one was built wrong.

Pip Garland, who is six and has walked beside me since the library, holds my lamp while I eat. He holds it with both hands and does not look away from it once. I notice that.

volumes.title: Out of Candles
volumes.text:
Below Market Square the Emberwick Lantern Parade goes down Quay Hill, which is steep and faces the sea wind. I walk last, being the Tail-Lamp, and so I am the one who sees the Pike go dark.

It happens a hoop at a time. The Quay’s green fish has fourteen candles in it, and the long wait at the top of the town has burned them to nothing. Head, then fins, then the tail goes grey, and eight fishermen stand in the road holding fourteen feet of unlit paper. I have been handing out candle ends all night and have nine left. I give them all. It needs five more.

Nobody speaks. The belly of the Owl opens, and a Fell Gate carrier climbs out with five of her own candles in his fist. He says the Owl sees well enough in the dark. I say nothing about it.

volumes.title: Rain at the Bridge Foot
volumes.text:
It begins to rain as the head of the Lantern Parade reaches the flat by the river. I am Odo Fenn, the Tail-Lamp, last of all, with a boy of six and his jam-jar lantern walking at my elbow, and we both turn our collars up.

Rain is hard on paper. The stars go first, then the paper drum from the school. Tin and turnip and glass do better. Ahead of us the Owl of Fell Gate, who lent five of her candles to her old rival on Quay Hill, is sagging at one wing, and I watch two of the Pike’s fishermen leave their poles, without being asked, and get a shoulder under it.

So they come to the Ember bridge like that, the Owl held up by the Quay and the Pike lit by Fell Gate, arguing the whole way about whose fault the weather is.

volumes.title: Wide Enough for One
volumes.text:
The Ember bridge is the end of the Lantern Parade, and it is wide enough for one great lantern at a time. I know, because I am the Tail-Lamp and have stood at the back of this argument for twenty years.

Tonight there is no argument. The Owl of Fell Gate has a broken wing and the Pike of the Quay is carrying it. They cannot be got apart without dropping somebody. So they go onto the bridge together, sideways, the Owl first by a beak and the Pike wrapped round her like a scarf, and the whole town goes quiet, and then laughs, and then claps.

Mrs Garland of the Committee asks me, as the oldest officer present, which of them led. I tell her I was at the back and could not see. It is entered in the minutes that way.

volumes.title: Counting Them In
volumes.text:
On the longest night of the year, Emberwick hangs its lanterns along the parapet of the Ember bridge, so that the river carries the light down to the sea and the dark knows it is expected to turn. I am Odo Fenn, Tail-Lamp of the parade. I count the lanterns out at the top of the town and in at the bottom.

Two hundred and six went out. I walk the parapet in the rain. Turnips, tin moons, the paper ones gone to lace but still hung up. The Owl and the Pike are propped together at the middle arch, steaming gently. Two hundred and five.

I count again. Then something knocks against my knee. Pip Garland, aged six, is holding up his jam jar, still alight, never once out since the library. He could not reach the parapet. I lift him, and he hangs it himself.

volumes.title: Putting Out the Lamp
volumes.text:
The parade is over, and the Tail-Lamp walks home last. That is me, Odo Fenn, tinsmith, going back up through Emberwick alone at ten o’clock on the longest night, with the rain easing and the bridge behind me still gold from end to end.

There is work even now. On Quay Hill I find a mitten, and in Market Square a cornet mouthpiece and a child’s scarf. At the corner by the library the wind has dropped. The lamp in the long window is still burning, and I lift my hat to it.

Twenty years is a fair turn. Next winter I will make a second lamp, small, with a horn window and a good hood, for a boy who can keep a jam jar alight in the rain. At my own door on Fell Gate I open my lamp and blow it out. Tomorrow is longer by a minute.

volumes.title: Five White Potatoes
volumes.text:
I am Ivy Tarn, of the Lowlands. I have judged flower shows for thirty-one summers, and I was told on the platform at Emberwick that theirs is a friendly one. I have learned to count my pencils when I hear that.

The tent stands on the water meadow by the Ember. By nine the Secretary, a Mrs Thrupp with a whistle, had cleared out the exhibitors, and I was alone with forty-one classes, a steward, and the smell of trodden grass and onions.

Class One, five white potatoes. People think one judges size. One judges sameness: five potatoes like five brothers, clean-skinned, shallow in the eye. The best dish belonged to a Mr Septimus Cray. I wrote First on the card. The steward breathed in sharply and said Mrs Lobb would have something to say. I asked who Mrs Lobb was. He only looked towards the marrows.

volumes.title: The Longest Bean
volumes.text:
Class Six at the Emberwick Flower Show is for the longest runner bean, and I, Ivy Tarn, the visiting judge, measured nineteen of them before ten o’clock with a steel rule, which I carry in my own bag.

A long bean is a simple thing to judge and a hard thing to judge fairly. Growers hang weights on them. They bind them to laths. One bean on the bench was straight as a curtain rod and still showed the marks of the string. I did not mark it down. The schedule says longest, not most natural, and a judge who invents rules is worse than an exhibitor who bends them.

It measured twenty-two inches and a quarter. First, to Mrs Hetty Lobb. Mr Cray’s bean, at twenty-two exactly, took Second. The steward told me the two of them have not spoken since a certain marrow, forty years ago.

volumes.title: Dahlias and an Earwig
volumes.text:
Class Twelve, six dahlias, any variety. I am Ivy Tarn, judge for the day at the Emberwick Flower Show, and by half past ten I had reached the cut flowers, where the tent smells less of onion.

There were seven vases. Six were good. The seventh was the kind of exhibit a judge sees perhaps one year in five: six blooms of a dark red, every petal in its place, the stems dead straight in a plain green vase. I bent to look into the heart of the largest, and an earwig walked out, crossed the petals, and regarded me. I have never marked down for an earwig. He had as much right there as I did.

First, without difficulty. The card under the vase said Mrs H. Lobb. I began to see that I would be hearing two names all day, hers and Mr Cray’s, turn and turn about.

volumes.title: The Heaviest Marrow
volumes.text:
There is a class at every show that the town really comes for. At Emberwick it is Class Twenty, the heaviest marrow, and I, Ivy Tarn, who had come from the Lowlands to judge, was warned about it by four separate people before I reached the bench.

Mr Septimus Cray and Mrs Hetty Lobb have taken First and Second in it, in one order or the other, for forty years. Their marrows lay side by side on straw like two green pigs. The steward and I lifted each onto the scale. Cray, thirty-eight pounds nine ounces. Lobb, thirty-eight pounds seven.

There was a third. It was pale, lopsided and enormous, and its card was written in pencil: T. Wicket, aged 11. Forty-one pounds three ounces. I weighed it twice more, because I could see what it was going to cost somebody. Then I wrote First on the pencilled card.

volumes.title: Not According to Schedule
volumes.text:
The hardest thing a show judge writes is three letters. I am Ivy Tarn, and I wrote them at Emberwick on a Saturday in August, at Class Twenty-Four, sweet peas, nine stems.

The best vase on the bench was not in doubt. Lavender and cream, long in the stem, four flowers to each and still with the dew on. They belonged to a Mr Anselm Pye, who the steward said had shown sweet peas for thirty years and never had a card. I counted the stems for form’s sake. Then I counted again. Ten.

The schedule says nine. An exhibit with ten is Not According to Schedule and cannot be placed. I did not make the rule and I will not break it. I wrote N.A.S. on his card in small letters and gave First to a decent vase of pink. Then I stood there longer than a judge should.

volumes.title: The Aspidistra
volumes.text:
Class Thirty at the Emberwick Flower Show is for a pot plant, foliage, and it had three entries, which in a class with three prizes takes some of the strain off a judge. I am that judge: Ivy Tarn, thirty-one years at it.

There was a fern. There was a young palm. And there was an aspidistra in a brown glazed pot, taller than the steward, with a luggage label tied to it that said: Property of the Station Waiting Room. Please Return. He told me it had been shown every year since the show began. It has never won. It is always Third. People, he said, would be upset by anything else.

I looked it over properly all the same. The leaves had been washed, I think with milk. The fern was the better plant and took First. The aspidistra took Third, and seemed to me to expect it.

volumes.title: Gardens on Plates
volumes.text:
I have judged in the Lowlands for thirty-one years, and I, Ivy Tarn, do not hand out prizes to be kind. So when the Secretary of the Emberwick Flower Show told me that in Class Thirty-Six, a miniature garden on a dinner plate, exhibitors under ten, it was the custom to give every child a First, I said that I could not.

There were fourteen plates. Moss lawns, a pond made of a pocket mirror, a gravel path of lentils. One had a live snail, which during judging left its own garden and began on the next.

I took an hour over them, longer than over the marrows. Then I wrote fourteen cards by hand, each different and each true. Best Pond. Straightest Path. Bravest Use of Moss. Most Generous Snail. Mrs Thrupp read them through twice and said it was irregular. Then she pinned them up herself.

volumes.title: Twenty-Three Pots of Jam
volumes.text:
A flower show judge at a small show is expected to judge the jam as well. I am Ivy Tarn; I was handed a teaspoon at noon in the tent at Emberwick, and shown Class Forty, one pot of soft-fruit jam, twenty-three entries.

One tastes each. There is no other way. One looks first: the set, the colour against the light, whether the fruit has sunk. Then a little on the spoon, and a sip of water between. By the fifteenth pot, raspberry and strawberry had become the same word. The sixteenth was gooseberry, sharp and green-gold, and woke me up.

First to the gooseberry, entered by a Mr S. Cray, whose name I had already met among the potatoes, beans and marrows. I remarked to the steward that the man could evidently cook. He said Mr Cray had lived alone forty years and had had to learn.

volumes.title: An Objection Is Lodged
volumes.text:
At one o’clock, with the judging done and the tent still closed, the Committee of the Emberwick Flower Show met behind the tea urn to hear an objection. I, Ivy Tarn, the judge, was asked to attend. I brought my sandwich.

The objection was against the winning marrow in Class Twenty, grown by Tom Wicket, aged eleven. It was lodged by Mr Septimus Cray and seconded by Mrs Hetty Lobb, and the Secretary remarked that this was the first thing the two of them had agreed upon in forty years. Their ground was that the marrow had been raised on the compost heap behind the railway station, which was not a garden.

Mrs Thrupp read out Rule Three: grown by the exhibitor. Nothing about where. The Committee voted. The objection failed, seven to none, with the objectors abstaining side by side, wearing the same expression.

volumes.title: The Tent Opens
volumes.text:
The public is let into the Emberwick Flower Show at two o’clock, and a judge with any sense is out of the tent by five to. I, Ivy Tarn, stayed. I wanted to see the marrow bench.

It was hot under the canvas, and the wasps had found the jam. People went straight to the cards, as they always do, and only afterwards looked at the flowers. At the marrows stood a small boy with a First card, and on either side of him the two growers he had beaten, Mr Cray and Mrs Lobb, who had not exchanged a word since long before he was born.

They were questioning him about feeding. Washing-up water, said Tom Wicket, and the tea leaves from the station. Mr Cray wrote that down. Mrs Lobb asked Mr Cray, quite sharply, for the loan of his pencil. He gave it to her.

volumes.title: Shillings in Envelopes
volumes.text:
Prizes at the Emberwick Flower Show are given out at four, from a trestle by the tent door: a shilling in an envelope for a First, sixpence for a Second, and four silver cups that go home for a year and come back polished. I am Ivy Tarn, who judged it. I was asked to hand them over, and did.

Mr Cray came up for his potatoes and his jam. Mrs Lobb came up for her bean and her dahlias. The Station Waiting Room was called for its aspidistra, and a porter collected the threepence. Fourteen children received a shilling each and compared cards all the way back.

Then the Marrow Tankard, pewter, forty years on one of two mantelpieces. Tom Wicket needed both arms for it. Mr Cray and Mrs Lobb led the clapping, slightly out of time, each watching to see that the other did not stop first.

volumes.title: The Tenth Stem
volumes.text:
The last prize at the Emberwick Flower Show is the cup for Best in Show, and I, Ivy Tarn, the judge, gave it to Mrs Hetty Lobb’s six red dahlias. Mr Cray carried the cup to her cart, her arms being full. They were talking about tea leaves.

One thing remained. Rule Nineteen allows the judge a single card of her own, for any exhibit, in or out of schedule. Mr Anselm Pye’s sweet peas had been ruled out for having ten stems where the class wanted nine. I took out the tenth, stood it in an egg cup, and set my card against it. He read it for a long time.

I caught the six o’clock train. On the seat beside me sat a marrow, a small one, for eating, with a label in two different hands. I have judged friendlier shows. I have not judged a better.
